title: On Kicking Rocks and Bruising Butts
excerpt: I’m a Bible college dropout with an unsatisfied fetish for the well-turned phrase. This blog is my attempt to hurl myself into the gaping maw of the existential abyss we call the internet and pray that at least a few scraps of me…
text: I’m a Bible college dropout with an unsatisfied fetish for the well-turned phrase. This blog is my attempt to hurl myself into the gaping maw of the existential abyss we call the internet and pray that at least a few scraps of me make it back into daylight. If lines like that aren’t too stilted or heavy-handed for you, maybe some part of me might affect some part of you (hopefully for the better) should you stick around. Today’s thought is about humility. I am often humbled by my mental health. Sometimes by how little I know about relationships, despite believing I’m more socially aware than most men. Often by poverty — which, in America, looks like a whiny fifty-year-old man complaining about his high-tech business while typing a blog post on his third smartphone, sitting comfortably in central heating and air, in front of a widescreen TV, with two prescription-fed cats in his lap. But hey, the couch is secondhand and I fit a government profile. So this must be what suffering feels like, right? Sure, even the homeless have TikTok pages, but that’s not the kind of humility on my mind tonight. The humility of failure — big or small — unites the rich and the poor, the first-world and the developing world. Whether you’re trying to become the first man to die on Mars and your rockets keep exploding in full view of humanity, or you’re trying to kick a rock farther than the other starving boy in the village who somehow has all the athletic talent, and you whiff-kick yourself straight into a bruised tailbone… every one of us has had to haul our proverbial backsides up from the dirt and try again at being somebody. I have ambitions big enough to end scarcity the world over and make humanity an interplanetary species — more than that, pioneers of the farthest reaches of the universe. If God and the cosmos are on my side, much of this could even happen during my lifetime. And yet today I was defeated by a half-page flyer. My ADHD turned finishing an already 99% complete bit of advertising into an insurmountable task. So I procrastinated and wrote this post instead, which I suppose is exactly what any author worth his salt would do. I’ll end this short thought by encouraging you to keep picking yourself up, dusting off your bruises, and giving it another go. One day you just might get what you want — and besides, that rock won’t kick itself.

title: Changing Meds Again
excerpt: I’m changing meds again. Lately I can’t leave the house without forgetting something essential. Not once in a while—every time. Wallet, phone, something I needed to return, whatever it is, it stays behind. I’m dropping things,…
text: I’m changing meds again. Lately I can’t leave the house without forgetting something essential. Not once in a while—every time. Wallet, phone, something I needed to return, whatever it is, it stays behind. I’m dropping things, running into furniture, mistiming steps like I’m out of sync with my own body. It’s subtle, but persistent. Enough to notice. Enough to know it’s time for an adjustment. Meanwhile, word has been getting out. The phone repairs I was quietly doing for friends have started expanding—friends of friends, then people I don’t really know. It’s been steady, and mostly manageable. And then came the flood of gear. Out of nowhere, people started handing me used tech—old consoles, routers, office hardware. No explanations, just “figured you could use this.” All told, about $2,000 worth of repairable or resellable stuff. I didn’t ask for it. It just showed up. So here I am. Switching meds. Forgetting basics. Slowly building a small tech salvage operation out of good timing, word of mouth, and whatever this current phase of life is. Not sure what direction this is heading in, but it feels like movement. And that’s enough, for now. Repair, Resell, Recycle! Pieced together with hope, hustle, and ChatGPT.

title: Sleep: The Final Boss of Recovery
excerpt: I’ve got the CPAP. I’ve got the sleeping pills. I even gave up my beloved evening Scotch. Latuda knocks me out, sure—but leaves me so restless I’m ready to burrow through the mattress and into the floorboards. And still, I wake…
text: I’ve got the CPAP. I’ve got the sleeping pills. I even gave up my beloved evening Scotch. Latuda knocks me out, sure—but leaves me so restless I’m ready to burrow through the mattress and into the floorboards. And still, I wake up feeling like I never slept at all. Sleep has become the last missing puzzle piece in my recovery, and like most final pieces, it’s doing its best to be elusive. Trazodone? That was a cruel joke. Three days awake. Three. Days. No one with schizophrenia should ever be forced to test the structural integrity of their sanity by staying awake for that long. I was told it would help. It didn’t. It hurt. A lot. Eventually, I found something that works—well, “works” in air quotes. It gets me to sleep, but it doesn’t undo the fragmented rest Latuda leaves behind. And let’s not forget I’m juggling twenty pills a day. There’s no such thing as an uncomplicated night of sleep when your med list looks like a CVS receipt. Then came Seroquel. Seroquel is an antipsychotic that allegedly helps with sleep. In reality? I didn’t sleep through the entire month of January. And I’m not talking “restless nights” or “light sleep.” I’m talking should’ve-just-played-PlayStation-until-dawn levels of insomnia. And February? Nearly as bad. I eventually crawled back to Latuda. Had I waited longer, I might’ve crawled somewhere less voluntary—like the psych ward. This was all happening during the final weeks of my business accelerator, when we gave our closing presentations. Also during this time, I went from working a half-shift a week at Goodwill to three full days. The money’s nice. The toll on my body and business? Not so much. Add 15 pounds of stress weight, a medication hangover that lasted until May, and the general chaos of trying to bootstrap a business while managing schizophrenia… and, well, I’m still here. And the website is so close to launching I can taste the HTML. No, I won’t have all my services up yet. But every iPhone repair I offer via mail-in service will be live. I call my shipping packaging RestoreBox™, and my ultrasonic cleaning service RestorePort Soniclean™. I’m not 100% sold on that name, but it does what it needs to do for now—just like me. Progress is slow, frustrating, and honestly a little messy. But it’s progress. And that’s something to feel good enough about today. Repair, Resell, Recycle! This post held together with duct tape, determination, and ChatGPT.

title: Still Clinically Well Adjusted (Mostly)
excerpt: May 2025 Check-In from the Founder of WeRestore.Tech Hey friends. It’s been a minute. Actually… since December. Life has been a whirlwind of solder fumes, secondhand retail shifts, broken phone screens, and learning everything I…
text: May 2025 Check-In from the Founder of WeRestore.Tech Hey friends. It’s been a minute. Actually… since December. Life has been a whirlwind of solder fumes, secondhand retail shifts, broken phone screens, and learning everything I didn’t know about running a business. I’ve been working extra hours at Goodwill trying to squeeze out every dollar I can before the equipment I need jumps in price from incoming tariffs. Startup life has this funny way of never really letting you stop being a startup. I think I’ll spend the rest of my life just trying to launch a simple website. But there’s good news too. The Blaze Accelerator was amazing. I’m still in touch with my cohort — a handful of brilliant, gritty, oddball builders like me. That community has kept me going when I started second-guessing myself (which, let’s be real, is a daily hobby). Even better? The grant came through. That money helped me incorporate as an official LLC — Dartel & Son dba: WeRestore.Tech — and snag some of the tools I was dreaming about when all this was just a crazy idea. I’m finally seeing a little snowball effect from word-of-mouth repairs, and the workbench is staying busy. That part feels real. It feels earned. The web store? That’s been a beast of its own. I’d never touched WordPress before this, and while the learning curve hasn’t been insurmountable, I definitely donated a chunk of my budget to broken themes and services I didn’t end up using. (RIP to that $59 “lifetime access” promise.) Add in a banking setup that’s still somehow stuck in a bureaucratic coma, and you start to get the picture. But we’re here. Still building. Still dreaming. Still clinically well adjusted. More updates soon — I promise. Until then, thanks for being part of this ride. — Curtis Founder, WeRestore.Tech Fixing what’s broken, from gadgetry to sanity. Repair, Resell, Recycle! This post built with grit, glitches, and ChatGPT.

title: Synergies Works Blaze Accelerator
excerpt: Yesterday marked the last day of the Blaze Business Accelerator for Entrepreneurs with Disabilities. It was Pitch Day—the grand finale. Four minutes to present my business and two minutes of Q&A. When the event recording goes…
text: Yesterday marked the last day of the Blaze Business Accelerator for Entrepreneurs with Disabilities. It was Pitch Day—the grand finale. Four minutes to present my business and two minutes of Q&A. When the event recording goes live, I’ll update this post with a link so you can witness my transformation into a 1980s monotone robot—a robot whose sole mission is to lull unsuspecting viewers into the nap of a lifetime. Do robots know when they’re making fools of themselves? Because there was some stammering I would gladly erase from my memory banks. But it was an amazing experience all the same. I would do it over again a thousand times . But Blaze wasn’t just about pitches. It was about people. My cohort—an extraordinary group of dreamers and hustlers—became family. Over nine weeks, we built more than businesses. It wasn’t all smooth sailing for me. My disability sometimes got in the way. A medication change and the side effects of the previous medication, and I missed a few sessions. I kept waiting for the “We regret to inform you…” email, but it never came. Either they saw my potential, or they just forgot to update the roster. I’ll take it. Blaze wasn’t a lecture series—it was a full-on boot camp for your brain and business. Each week brought new challenges, field experiments, and “why-didn’t-I-think-of-this-sooner” moments. The end feels abrupt, like finishing a great book only to realize the last chapter is missing. But instead of sadness, I feel grateful—grateful for the tools I’ve gained, the confidence I’ve built, and the amazing people I’ve met. For anyone wondering if a program like this is worth it, let me say this: absolutely. Blaze pushed my business, WeRestore.Tech, forward in ways I didn’t think possible. It reminded me that I’m not alone in this journey. I had to put a lot of projects on hold to get the most out of the program. I still work at my local Goodwill as a fallback so time was a precious commodity. Getting the website up is now priority one. So, here’s to Blaze, my incredible cohort, and all the entrepreneurs willing to put their reputations on the line to make their mark on the world—even when the odds seem stacked against them. I’m going to make several posts in the coming weeks about some of what I learned. Stay tuned for the pitch recording (and nap potential), and if you’re curious about the highs, lows, and lessons of building a business while living with schizophrenia, hit that follow button. There’s plenty more to come. Repair, Resell, Recycle! This post fueled by chaos, late nights, and ChatGPT.

title: Solving e-polution, one repair at a time—because sanity is overrated.
excerpt: Hi there! Welcome to the first-ever post on Clinically Well Adjusted, where I’ll share my journey building WeRestore.Tech from scratch, all while navigating life with schizophrenia and making a sustainable tech business a…
text: Hi there! Welcome to the first-ever post on Clinically Well Adjusted, where I’ll share my journey building WeRestore.Tech from scratch, all while navigating life with schizophrenia and making a sustainable tech business a reality. If you’re reading this, you’re probably here for one of three reasons: You’re curious about how a disabled entrepreneur is bootstrapping a business. You just want to know if I can fix your phone. You took a wrong turn on the internet but decided to stick around anyway (great choice, by the way). Let me break it down for you: life isn’t simple when you’re living on disability income, running a business from your kitchen table, and trying to save the planet one gadget at a time. But here’s the thing—it doesn’t have to be simple to be worth it. Through this blog, I’ll share my repair hacks, business wins (and fails), mental health ups and downs, and the occasional bad pun. My YouTube channel will give you the behind-the-scenes chaos—think tech tutorials, real talk about entrepreneurship, and a front-row seat to my experiments in not losing my mind while fixing yours (your tech, that is). Why am I doing this? Because being real about the struggle is what makes the story worth telling. Too many people on the schizophrenia spectrum are told to lower their expectations of living a productive life. I want my story to inspire hope—for you or for someone else—to believe in the possibility of a better life. Also, because I’ve Googled ‘how to start a sustainable tech business with no money’ way too many times, and it’s about time someone wrote the real guide. Stick around for repair tips, sustainability insights, and a few laughs along the way. After all, the world might be a mess, but your phone doesn’t have to be. Thanks for joining me on this wild ride—here’s to trying, failing, and trying again, with style. Repair, Resell, Recycle! This post was powered by stubbornness, coffee, and ChatGPT.
